title: Moses runs (Exodus 2:11–22)
hookLine: he kills an Egyptian, flees, and becomes a stranger in a strange land
carry: a stranger in a strange land

cards: Moses grows up in the palace: Egyptian clothes, Egyptian schooling, a princess for a mother. But he knows, somehow, who his people are. One day, a grown man, he goes out and watches them carrying their loads.

He sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own. Moses looks this way and that way, sees no one, kills the Egyptian, and hides the body in the sand. It's the first thing the adult Moses does in the Bible.
Not a miracle. A killing, done in anger, in secret, with a glance over his shoulder.

teach.h: WHO MADE THEE A JUDGE OVER US?
teach.b: The next day he sees two Hebrews fighting, and tells the one in the wrong to stop. The man turns on him, in the King James Bible: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?"
Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian? So it's known.

Pharaoh wants him dead, and Moses runs, east out of Egypt, all the way to the land of Midian, and sits down by a well. Wells keep turning up in this story: Rebekah at one, Jacob and Rachel at another.
Seven sisters come to water their father's flock, and shepherds drive them off. Moses stands up for them and waters their flock.
At home they tell their father: an Egyptian rescued us. In Egypt he's a Hebrew. In Midian he's an Egyptian.
He belongs nowhere. The father takes him in, Moses marries one of the daughters, Zipporah, and they have a son.
Moses names him Gershom, saying: "I have been a stranger in a strange land." Ger is the Hebrew word for a stranger, a foreigner living among people not their own.
Christians and Jews have both struggled with the killing: was it justice, or rage?
In the book of Acts, Stephen retells it as Moses taking his people's side, supposing they would understand that God meant to free them by his hand; they didn't. The Bible doesn't settle it.
But it never forgets what Moses learned in Midian.

teach.h: I HAVE BEEN A STRANGER IN A STRANGE LAND.
teach.b: Israel's law will later say: don't oppress a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

how: Christians often draw on Moses's years as a stranger in Midian, and on the laws about strangers that follow from Israel's time in Egypt, when churches welcome immigrants and refugees.

s: Moses's first act as an adult in Exodus is a miracle
it's a killing, done in secret, after looking this way and that.
the sisters at the well thought Moses was an Egyptian
in Egypt a Hebrew, in Midian an Egyptian: he belongs nowhere.
the Bible clearly praises Moses for the killing
it doesn't settle it; readers have debated it for centuries.

games.q: you're Moses, a fugitive in Midian, sitting by a well. shepherds drive seven sisters away from the water. what do you do?
o: stay out of it; you're already in trouble.
stand up, help them, and water their flock.
games.why: he stands up and helps them. the man who couldn't stand injustice in Egypt can't stand it in Midian either, and this time no one dies.

practice: Remember a time you were the stranger, a new school, a new job, a new country, a room where you knew no one, and who helped.
Now think of someone around you who is new right now, a neighbor, a coworker, a family at school, and picture greeting them. If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Moses runs. After killing an Egyptian, he flees to Midian, marries, and names his son for what he has become: a stranger in a strange land.

orig.note: Hebrew: a stranger, a foreigner living among others. the first part of the name Gershom.

carryVoice: Your line: a stranger in a strange land. Moses knew that edge well. See you tomorrow.
